extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, comedy actors, and improv teachers
extracted.subtask_short: improv character creation and scene work
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and evaluative principles for playing characters and structuring scenes in improvisational theatre (short-form and long-form), including techniques for generating non-cliché characters, preserving dramatic cause-and-effect, and ending scenes effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Add cost to weak choices
rubrics_metrics.description: A weak choice can be made strong by adding a cost; classic heroes must make moral choices and if the “right” course of action is free of cost then stakes are lowered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a character initially refuses or makes a weak choice, raise its dramatic weight by attaching a cost or moral consequence so the decision matters. Example: in hero’s-journey terms, refusing the call becomes compelling if acceptance carries sacrifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify any character action (avoid 'my character wouldn't do that')
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost no action is beyond justification — any character is capable of any action; if the character does something new we see another side to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t hide behind the cliché that a character 'wouldn’t do that.' Instead, find or build a justification onstage (motivation, cost, history, status shift) and commit to it so the audience accepts the change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make binary choices affect a character
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary choices in improv will do provided one or other character is affected; if a choice (e.g., Sally is real or not) is made, it must have a profound effect on the other character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you pick one of two mutually exclusive realities, ensure the outcome changes a character’s emotional or status state so the choice has dramatic weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use status reversal and irony to raise stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning a character’s wish into something they did not want after all adds irony and emotional complexity (e.g., wish fulfilled but unwanted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reversals where getting what you want reveals an unexpected cost or loss of desire; this adds emotional layers and can be used to complicate scenes meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: If deadlock persists, have either character break it credibly
rubrics_metrics.description: If one character won’t break a deadlock, the other must, but such moves should be justified (e.g., weaken the resisting character or drop another character’s status).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choices to break stalemate should be motivated: weaken the resistor, have the other character change tactics/status, or introduce a believable reason for the turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismantling the scene sparingly and with justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulling the rug out from under the audience is acceptable occasionally, but compulsive originalism without justification damages the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveals that negate prior events (e.g., 'it was all a film' or 'it was a dream') often escape the need to develop story and should be used carefully; ensure any frame-break furthers character or story rather than avoids it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve expectations and avoid cancelling offers prematurely
rubrics_metrics.description: Canceling offers (abandoning previously established repeated behavior) in the beginning or middle creates confusion and is usually bad; canceling ends stories so should be reserved for endings or used with strong justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch what expectations you’ve raised; if a character repeatedly bullies someone, a sudden unmotivated apology cancels offers and confuses. Instead follow implications or provide a believable reason for change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow implications to a natural ending; don’t dismantle platform to end
rubrics_metrics.description: Great storytellers follow the implications of their offers to the end rather than pulling reversals just to end; canceling as a way to achieve an ending is weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the platform (established rules/details) as the basis to resolve problems. Endings should feel like the logical consequence of what came before (reincorporation, status shifts, irony), not an arbitrary dismantle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physicality and strong attitudes to justify and heighten scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Physicality (posture, gestures, tics) and clearly held attitudes create rich characters and provide justification, increasing emotional energy and audience investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concrete physical instructions (e.g., clasping hands, rounding back, bobbing head) to create believable character traits. Embody those traits consistently while the scene progresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain platform rules unless convincingly altered
rubrics_metrics.description: If a scene’s platform contains a rule (e.g., 'shoes must be bought and sold'), violating it without justification drops stakes; obedience to platform can be a source of story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either play out the platform’s consequences (raise stakes) or provide a strong, staged reason for breaking/altering the rule; otherwise the scene flattens when rules are casually ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change attitude to generate forward movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifting tactics (reasoning, pleading, threatening, destroying) can unlock new directions and reveal cause-and-effect in the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If bargaining stalls, vary emotional register and tactics to provoke new responses and keep momentum. Physical actions that escalate (e.g., destroying the shoes) can produce meaningful effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve cause-and-effect and ensure stories make sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginner improvisers should focus on maintaining causal logic so scenes develop naturally; populate the environment and play characters who are changed by events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure actions lead to believable consequences. Populate details to give opportunities for cause-effect chains; as instincts develop, vary expectations and surprise more confidently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop consequences from earlier actions to reveal character
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories work by developing consequences from earlier actions so they remain true to characters; don’t treat early events as throwaway introductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extend routines by following their logical consequences (e.g., villagers angry after monster slain), escalating or complicating them until a satisfying reversal or reincorporation completes the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposite technique: play the opposite of your obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid cliché and quickly invent fresh characters, identify the obvious adjectives for a role and then play their opposites (e.g., a courteous, uninterested parking inspector).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'what’s the opposite of my obvious?' and commit to that set of traits. The opposite must still be justified by the performer onstage; otherwise it reads as cleverness without grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme technique: take a stereotype as far as it will go
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than stopping at stereotype, exaggerate qualities to their limits to create characters who really care and drive strong, often short, scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Push traits to absurd consistency (e.g., a parking inspector who fines for insults or attempts to steal cash) to give other characters strong motives and audience amusement. Works well for short-form high-absurdity pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary technique: use a random prompt to inspire character detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a random word or obsession (derived arbitrarily) to give the character an unexpected dimension while still remaining in-role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the arbitrary element (dog, screenplay, cats, etc.) inform how the character behaves, but do not forget you are still a parking inspector/doctor/etc. Use the arbitrary as imaginative fodder rather than as an escape from role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overloading scenes with multiple novelty techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing opposite/extreme/arbitrary approaches together in a short form sketch can overload and confuse the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit simultaneous novelty devices in short-form. If multiple arbitraries meet, the scene risks being Wonderland without an Alice — include a straight man to give the audience access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play the straight man when needed (say what the audience is thinking)
rubrics_metrics.description: A straight man anchors the scene and expresses the audience’s perspective amid absurdity, making arbitrary characters accessible and funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a partner creates wacky offers, respond as the 'normal' person (pointing out incongruities) to channel audience reaction and help structure the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be affected and make characters affect others
rubrics_metrics.description: Arbitrary, opposite and extreme characters are most interesting when they affect people in big ways; being affected by partners makes scenes stronger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let your character react emotionally and physically to what others do; affect/response is central to improv: if a partner trivializes things, show being affected to create stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build characters with depth through group-created details
rubrics_metrics.description: Create characters collaboratively (name, voice, physical instructions) so performers can inhabit unfamiliar types and sustain them convincingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific, actionable directions ('cross your legs, tilt your chin, smoke a cigarette') rather than vague descriptors. Build characters slowly with group support so performers feel permission to commit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swap and perform others’ characters to develop versatility
rubrics_metrics.description: Having different improvisers play group-created characters shows how physicality and performance choices make a character distinct and builds a repertoire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick another’s character and play it; variations (gender, accent, gesture) will create fresh versions. The group-created catalog becomes tools players can reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commit fully to the character (sell it)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commitment is two-thirds of your job: if you don’t sell the character (movement, voice, belief), the audience won’t buy it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Push forward even when you feel silly. Overcoming instinct to pull back by doing more (stronger physicality, clearer choices) produces believable characters and audience buy-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create characters with dimension (surface vs inner life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dimensional characters show contrasts (e.g., Bond looks like a playboy but is a killer) so reveal contradictions and inner sides over time to engage audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, show glimpses of inner life, softer edges, or past history even in short scenes to make characters more moving and memorable. In long-form reuse characters to reveal new facets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch vs long-form: recognize limits and opportunities of each
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketch characters often only show surface; long-form affords revealing inner life over multiple appearances; short-form must find economical ways to hint at dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In sketches, rely on bold strokes but try to include a small revealing beat of inner life when feasible. Use recurring characters in long-form to develop emotional depth.
